note: Rav Dimi reported that once people forgot to bring a Torah scroll to the synagogue before Shabbat. The next day they spread sheets over posts along the way, carried the scroll to the synagogue, and read from it. The Gemara objects that they could not have spread sheets on Shabbat, since they would have had to carry them there; rather, they found sheets already spread on the posts, and brought the scroll along that path.
why: The Gemara has argued that neither Rabbi Yehuda nor Rabbi Yosei accepts a hanging partition for carrying on Shabbat, and asks whose view the incident in Tzippori followed. This is that incident, done on the authority of Rabbi Yishmael, son of Rabbi Yosei.

people.name: Rav Dimi
people.about: A Sage who came from the Land of Israel to Babylonia and reported this incident.

terms.meaning: Carrying an object through a public area is forbidden on Shabbat unless the area is enclosed by partitions that the law recognizes.
The handwritten parchment scroll of the Five Books of Moses, read in the synagogue on Shabbat.

note: During the water-pouring ceremony at the Temple, a Sadducee priest poured the water over his own feet instead of on the altar. In anger, all the people pelted him with their etrogim. That day a horn of the altar was damaged, and they sealed it with a lump of salt, not to make the altar fit for service but so that it would not be seen damaged.
why: The mishna has described the two basins for the water and wine libations, and that the one pouring water was told to raise his hand. The incident shows why; the Gemara then adds that an altar missing a horn is unfit for service, which is why the salt did not make it fit.

people.name: a Sadducee priest
people.about: Poured the water libation on his feet and was pelted by the crowd.

terms.meaning: A member of a Jewish group of the Second Temple period that rejected many traditions of the Sages.
A ceremony on the festival of Sukkot in which water was poured out on the altar.
A citron, a lemon-like fruit held during prayers on Sukkot; the plural is etrogim.
One of the raised corners of the Temple altar.
